literal: Thereafter rebels often submitted.
idiomatic: Rebels then often came back in.

literal: Gaozu approved and, turning to the attendant ministers, said: "The Prince of Jiangyang is fully fit for great responsibility.
idiomatic: Gaozu approved and told his ministers, "The Prince of Jiangyang is fit for heavy trust."

literal: The imperial carriage toured north to Ye; the Gaoche all surrendered; Heng and Shu were pacified.
idiomatic: The throne toured north to Ye; the Gaoche surrendered; Heng and Shu were quiet.

literal: Because the Gaoche had stirred rebellion, Ji repeatedly memorialized to accept blame; Gaozu answered with a gracious edict to reassure him.
idiomatic: Ji kept memorializing to take blame for the Gaoche revolt; Gaozu answered with a gracious edict.

literal: In Shizong's time he was appointed General Who Subdues the Barbarians and Inspector of Qingzhou; transferred to General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Hengzhou; he entered court as Director of Revenue.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he was general who subdues the barbarians and Qingzhou inspector, then general who pacifies the north and Hengzhou inspector, then director of revenue.

literal: While Ji was in Qingzhou the people starved; he had household slaves take commoners' daughters as wives and concubines and also made free men into maidservants; the censorate impeached him and he was dismissed from office and title.
idiomatic: In Qingzhou, while the people starved, Ji's slaves took commoners' daughters and free men as servants; the censors impeached him and he lost office and title.

literal: Later Grand Marshal Gao Zhao campaigned against Shu; Shizong made Ji General Who Pacifies the East to hold Xu and Yang in check.
idiomatic: Later Grand Marshal Gao Zhao marched on Shu; Shizong made Ji general who pacifies the east to hold Xu and Yang.

literal: When Shizong died, the armies withdrew.
idiomatic: When Shizong died, the armies withdrew.

literal: When Empress Dowager Ling held court, Ji's son Cha had first married the empress dowager's younger sister; Ji was restored to Director of the Masters of Writing and his original enfeoffment, and shortly made Palace Attendant and Commander of the Army.
idiomatic: When Empress Dowager Ling ruled, Cha had married her sister; Ji was restored to director of the Masters of Writing and his fief, then palace attendant and army commander.

literal: He was also made Special Grandee and Rapid Cavalry General, Palace Attendant and Army Commander as before.
idiomatic: He was also special grandee and rapid cavalry general, retaining palace attendant and army command.

literal: Ji repeatedly memorialized to decline firmly; this was granted.
idiomatic: Ji memorialized again and again to decline; the court allowed it.

literal: Another edict restored the former appointments.
idiomatic: Another edict restored the former appointments.

literal: Grand Preceptor Prince of Gaoyang Yong, Grand Tutor Prince of Qinghe Yi, Grand Guardian Prince of Guangping Huai, and the eight seats of the Secretariat memorialized to review Ji's merit in the Taihe era in comforting the Gaoche and pacifying the four garrisons, adding a thousand five hundred households to his fief.
idiomatic: Grand Preceptor Yong of Gaoyang, Grand Tutor Yi of Qinghe, Grand Guardian Huai of Guangping, and the eight secretariat seats asked to review Ji's Taihe service with the Gaoche and four garrisons and add fifteen hundred households.

literal: Ji again memorialized to decline; an edict permitted reduction by five hundred households.
idiomatic: Ji declined again; the throne cut the grant by five hundred households.

literal: Because her son Cha was a marriage connection, Empress Dowager Ling often visited Ji's house with Suzong, set out wine in high feast, and bestowed gifts beyond measure.
idiomatic: As Cha was kin by marriage, Ling often feasted at Ji's house with Suzong and heaped gifts on him.

literal: Shortly he was made additional Palace Attendant, General of Rapid Cavalry, and Bearer of Ceremonial Equal to the Three Excellencies, Special Grandee and Army Commander as before.
idiomatic: Soon he was also palace attendant, general of rapid cavalry, and bearer of ceremonial equal to the Three Excellencies, keeping special grandee and army command.

literal: His enfeoffment was changed to Prince of Jingzhao.
idiomatic: He was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Jingzhao.

literal: Ji had been ill for years, nursing himself at home; whenever Empress Dowager Ling and Suzong toured outside, they had him helped in to hold the inner palace.
idiomatic: Ji had been ill for years at home; whenever Ling and Suzong left the capital, they had him carried in to guard the inner palace.

literal: At seasonal feasts he forced himself to attend though ill.
idiomatic: At seasonal feasts he dragged himself in though sick.

literal: He was moved to Minister of Works, Palace Attendant as before.
idiomatic: He was made minister of works, retaining palace attendant.

literal: Broad and easy in bearing, he was called an elder.
idiomatic: Easy in manner, he was called an elder.

literal: At the end of Shengui his son Cha came to power; he was transferred to Minister of the Masses, still additional Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Late in Shengui, when Cha rose, he was made minister of the masses, still palace attendant.

literal: As a frontier prince and long-serving old noble, in Gaozu's time he had held eminent posts inside and outside; favor had already been great.
idiomatic: A frontier prince and long-serving noble, he had held high posts under Gaozu inside and outside court.

literal: When Empress Dowager Ling held court he entered her inner circle, also sat in the Secretariat, passed through the terrace offices, and Cha held heavy power—glory for a generation.
idiomatic: Under Ling he entered her inner circle and the secretariat, rose through the terrace, while Cha held power—glory for an age.

literal: Ji repeatedly memorialized to yield rank, begging to give the Ministry of the Masses to Cui Guang.
idiomatic: Ji repeatedly asked to step down and give the ministry of the masses to Cui Guang.

literal: An edict sent Palace Attendant Prince of Anfeng Yanming and Drafting Attendant of the Yellow Gate Lu Tong to urge him earnestly.
idiomatic: The throne sent Yanming of Anfeng and Lu Tong of the yellow gate to urge him.

literal: Ji again memorialized to decline firmly; he was transferred to Grand Guardian, Palace Attendant as before, with additional rear guard music; he repeatedly memorialized to decline and was not permitted.
idiomatic: Ji declined again; he was made grand guardian, still palace attendant, with rear guard music; he kept declining and was refused.

literal: An edict said: "At the great seasonal festivals, rites require court celebration; kin, elders, and the honored ought by principle to receive special treatment.
idiomatic: An edict said: "At great festivals the court celebrates; kin and elders deserve special honor.

literal: The prince's rank is high and his years many; he may follow the precedent of Prince Jian of Qi commandery—after court, led to a seat, exempt from bowing and prostration."
idiomatic: His rank is high and his years many; follow Prince Jian of Qi—after audience, seat him and spare bowing."

literal: He was transferred to Grand Tutor, Palace Attendant as before.
idiomatic: He was made grand tutor, still palace attendant.

literal: Repeated declinations were not granted; envoys were again sent to urge him, and then he accepted.
idiomatic: He kept declining; envoys urged again; then he accepted.

literal: At that time Cha held the power of life and death, authority and favor his own; students and former subordinates filled the ministries; on the day of investiture senders filled the court—contemporaries took it for glory, men of judgment for fear.
idiomatic: Cha then held life and death in his hand; clients filled the ministries; on investiture day the court turned out to see him—some called it glory, the wise called it dread.

literal: The Imperial Kitchen supplied wine and food for guests.
idiomatic: The imperial kitchen supplied feast and wine.

literal: Another edict ordered him to ride in a hand-drawn carriage to the court hall, two men supporting him; ritual rank equaled the Chancellor Prince of Gaoyang.
idiomatic: Another edict let him ride a hand-drawn carriage to court, two men at his arms; ritual rank matched Chancellor Yong of Gaoyang.

literal: Later he was appointed Bearer of Credentials, Palace Attendant, Grand Preceptor, Grand Marshal, Recorder of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing, Commander-in-Chief, directing armies of the western circuit.
idiomatic: Later he bore credentials as palace attendant, grand preceptor, grand marshal, recorder of the Masters of Writing, and commander-in-chief of the western armies.

literal: On the day the armies set out, the imperial carriage came to see them off; the whole court sent them off; rewards were beyond counting.
idiomatic: When the armies marched, the throne came to see them off; the whole court followed; rewards were beyond count.

literal: He was transferred to Grand Marshal, Palace Attendant, Grand Preceptor, Recorder of the Masters of Writing, and Commander-in-Chief as before.
idiomatic: He was made grand marshal, keeping palace attendant, grand preceptor, recorder, and command.

literal: Shortly an edict ordered withdrawal of the armies.
idiomatic: Soon an edict recalled the armies.

literal: Ji memorialized asking to return to Jiangyang; the edict followed this.
idiomatic: Ji asked to return to Jiangyang; the throne agreed.

literal: Cha, Ji's eldest son, styled Bojun, pet name Yecha.
idiomatic: Cha, Ji's eldest son, styled Bojun, pet name Yecha.

literal: In Shizong's time he was appointed Outer Office Gentleman.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he was outer-office gentleman.

literal: When Empress Dowager Ling held court, as son-in-law he was made Direct-palace Scattered Cavalier Attendant.
idiomatic: When Ling ruled, as son-in-law he was direct-palace scattered cavalier attendant.

literal: Cha's wife was made Lady of Xinping commandery; later moved to Lady of Fengyi commandery and appointed Lady Attendant-in-Ordinary.
idiomatic: Cha's wife was Lady of Xinping, then Lady of Fengyi and lady attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: Because of this Cha's intent and power grew daily; shortly he was moved to Scattered Cavalier Attendant, Vice Director of the Honored Grandee Office, Director of the Palace Food Service, then Honored Grandee.
idiomatic: His power grew; soon he was scattered cavalier attendant, vice director of the honored grandee office, director of palace food service, then honored grandee.

literal: Cha's daughter died young; Empress Dowager Ling's edict said: "Cha's eldest daughter, nearly of hairpin age, suddenly met early death; grief is doubled; she may be granted the title of District Lady.
idiomatic: Cha's daughter died young; Ling's edict said: "Cha's eldest daughter, nearly of age, died suddenly; grief is doubled; grant her district lady."

literal: Shortly he was moved to Palace Attendant, other offices as before, with additional Army Commander.
idiomatic: Soon he was palace attendant with other offices unchanged and additional army command.

literal: Once in the Secretariat he also held overall command of the forbidden troops and was deeply trusted by Empress Dowager Ling.
idiomatic: In the secretariat he also held the forbidden troops and was deeply trusted by Ling.

literal: Grand Tutor Prince of Qinghe Yi, as a kinsman and worthy assisting in government, took part in deciding affairs of state; because Cha relied on favor and was arrogant beyond measure, with ambition without limit, Yi restrained him by law.
idiomatic: Grand Tutor Yi of Qinghe, kinsman and worthy, shared government; Cha, swollen with favor and limitless ambition, Yi checked by law.

literal: Cha looked down on his person and constantly wished to drive him out.
idiomatic: Cha despised him and kept trying to oust him.

literal: [8] Cha then had Direct-palace Gentleman Song Wei report that Director of the Dye Office Commandery-Commandant Han Wenshu plotted treason to set up Yi; Yi was placed under prohibition.
idiomatic: [8] Cha had direct-palace gentleman Song Wei accuse Han Wenshu, director of the dye office, of plotting to set up Yi; Yi was confined.

literal: Later exhaustive investigation found no substance; though Yi was released, he was still guarded by armed men in a separate lodge west of the palace.
idiomatic: Investigation found nothing; Yi was freed but still guarded in a lodge west of the palace.

literal: After a long while Cha feared Yi would in the end harm him and secretly plotted with Palace Attendant Liu Teng.
idiomatic: In time Cha feared Yi would destroy him and plotted secretly with Liu Teng.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling was then at Jiafu and had not entered the front hall; Teng falsely took chief food-service yellow-gate attendants Hu Xuandu and Hu Ding and charged Yi, saying Yi had promised Xuandu and the rest gold and silk to place poison in the imperial food to harm the emperor, himself hoping to become emperor and promising the Hu brothers wealth and honor.
idiomatic: Ling was at Jiafu, not in the front hall; Teng seized food-service attendants Hu Xuandu and Hu Ding and accused Yi of promising them gold to poison the emperor's food, seize the throne, and enrich the Hu brothers.

literal: Teng submitted the full report; Suzong heard it and believed; he then held court at Xianyang Hall.
idiomatic: Teng laid out the charge; Suzong believed it and held court at Xianyang Hall.

literal: Teng closed the Eternal Lane gate; Empress Dowager Ling could not go out.
idiomatic: Teng shut the Eternal Lane gate; Ling could not leave.

literal: Yi entered and met Cha behind Hanzhang Hall; wishing to enter the eastern gate of Huizhang, Cha shouted and would not allow it.
idiomatic: Yi entered and met Cha behind Hanzhang Hall; trying to enter Huizhang's eastern gate, Cha shouted him back.

literal: Yi said: "Do you wish to rebel?"
idiomatic: Yi said, "Do you mean to rebel?"

literal: Cha said: "Yuan Cha does not rebel; I mean to bind the rebel."
idiomatic: Cha said, "Yuan Cha does not rebel; I mean to bind the rebel."

literal: Cha ordered clan guards and direct-garrison men, some thirty, to seize Yi by robe and sleeve and take him into the eastern office of Hanzhang, with several tens guarding him.
idiomatic: Cha had some thirty clan guards seize Yi by the sleeves and drag him into Hanzhang's eastern office under guard.

literal: Teng, claiming an edict, summoned the excellencies and ministers to discuss the great-treason verdict; all feared Cha and none dared differ.
idiomatic: Teng, claiming an edict, called the excellencies to judge great treason; all feared Cha and none dissented.

literal: Only Vice Director of the Masters of Writing You Zhao held a different view.
idiomatic: Only Vice Director You Zhao disagreed.

literal: The account is in his biography.
idiomatic: His biography tells the rest.

literal: Cha and Teng took the excellencies' deliberation in to memorialize; shortly the matter was approved; in the middle of the night Yi was killed.
idiomatic: Cha and Teng submitted the verdict; it was approved; Yi was killed at midnight.

literal: Thereupon they forged an edict in which Empress Dowager Ling declined the regency.
idiomatic: They forged an edict in which Ling declined the regency.

literal: Cha then assisted in government with Grand Preceptor Prince of Gaoyang Yong and others, constantly on duty in the forbidden precinct; Suzong called him "uncle."
idiomatic: Cha then ruled with Yong of Gaoyang and others, always in the inner palace; Suzong called him uncle.

literal: From then on he monopolized the keys of state; great and small he decided; his authority shook inside and outside; the hundred offices walked in fear.
idiomatic: From then on he held every lever; great and small affairs were his; power shook court and realm; officials walked in fear.

literal: Prince of Zhongshan Xi, Inspector of Xiangzhou, memorialized in righteous uprising under the banner of punishing Cha; it came to nothing and he was executed.
idiomatic: Prince Xi of Zhongshan, Xiangzhou inspector, rose in righteous protest to punish Cha; he failed and was killed.

literal: Cha was shortly moved to Guards General, other offices as before.
idiomatic: Cha was soon made guards general with other offices unchanged.

literal: Later Empress Dowager Ling feasted with Suzong in Xilin Garden; at dusk returning to the palace, Right Guards General Xi Kangsheng again plotted against Cha and failed; he was executed.
idiomatic: Later Ling feasted with Suzong in Xilin Garden; at dusk, Right Guards General Xi Kangsheng plotted against Cha and was killed.

literal: The account is in his biography.
idiomatic: His biography tells the rest.

literal: Thereafter Suzong moved his residence to Huiyin Hall; Cha also entered and dwelt on the hall's right.
idiomatic: Afterward Suzong moved to Huiyin Hall; Cha lodged on its right.

literal: Being in close secrecy, he exhausted flattery to meet the sovereign's intent and thereby won favor and trust.
idiomatic: Close to the throne, he flattered without cease and won trust.

literal: Entering the forbidden precinct, he always had brave men carry swords before and behind; whether in public or private going and stopping, his guard grew stricter.
idiomatic: In the palace he kept armed braves before and behind; public or private, his guard grew heavier.

literal: Cha set wooden railings in the shed below the Thousand Autumns Gate; when he went in and out he sometimes rested within them; trusted men guarded against sudden attack; those who sought audience spoke to him only from afar.
idiomatic: Below the Thousand Autumns Gate he built a wooden pen; he rested there coming and going; trusted men watched against attack; petitioners spoke only from a distance.

literal: He enfeoffed his son Liang as Duke of Pingyuan commandery with a fief of a thousand households.
idiomatic: He enfeoffed his son Liang as duke of Pingyuan with a thousand households.

literal: At the investiture Suzong watched from the southern gate; he also granted imperial horses and a thousand bolts of silk.
idiomatic: At investiture Suzong watched from the southern gate and gave imperial horses and a thousand bolts of silk.

literal: At first, when Cha monopolized government, he affected feeling and adorned himself, laboring in humility toward scholars; he was somewhat concerned with the gains and losses of the time—but his talent was shallow and in the end he had no far-reaching achievement.
idiomatic: At first Cha affected modesty and courted scholars, even noting the times' faults—but his talent was shallow and nothing lasting came of it.

literal: Once he had his wish, he became arrogant and obstinate, addicted to wine and women, granting and seizing as whim dictated.
idiomatic: Once secure, he turned arrogant, drank, chased women, gave and took at whim.

literal: He made a private vault in the forbidden precinct and held it himself; treasures filled it to overflowing.
idiomatic: He built a private vault in the palace and stuffed it with treasure.

literal: [9] He also once had a woman lie in the food carriage, covered with a cloth, and had men carry her into the forbidden precinct; going out was the same; the direct guard knew but none dared speak.
idiomatic: [9] He once had a woman lie in the food cart, covered with cloth, and carried into the palace; the guard knew and dared not speak.

literal: Frivolous men who chased power served him with wine and women; aunts, sisters, and wives mingled in lewdness without distinction.
idiomatic: Men who chased favor served him with wine and sex; aunts, sisters, and wives mingled without shame.

literal: Government grew slack; statutes were not upheld; governors and garrison commanders were mostly unfit men.
idiomatic: Government slackened; law went unenforced; provincial and garrison posts went to the wrong men.

literal: Thereupon the realm fell into disorder.
idiomatic: The realm then fell into disorder.

literal: After Liu Teng died, guard and defense grew somewhat slack; Cha also relaxed somewhat; he often lodged outside, going out daily to roam and lingering in other towns.
idiomatic: After Liu Teng died, guards eased; Cha eased too, often sleeping out and roaming other towns.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling subtly perceived this.
idiomatic: Ling noticed in secret.

literal: Cha's habits had become constant; he no longer took precautions.
idiomatic: Habit had dulled Cha; he took no precautions.

literal: Those close to him remonstrated; Cha would not accept it.
idiomatic: Kin who warned him were ignored.

literal: In autumn of the fifth year of Zhenguang, Empress Dowager Ling said to Suzong before the ministers: "You have cut off me and my son, not letting me go back and forth to my boy—what use am I still?
idiomatic: In autumn, Zhenguang 5, Ling told Suzong before the court: "You wall me off from my son—of what use am I?

literal: Release me to leave the household; I will forever leave the human world and cultivate the Way at Songgao Xianju Temple.
idiomatic: Let me take the tonsure and leave the world for Songgao Xianju Temple."

literal: The late emperor's sacred discernment foresaw what was not yet manifest; he built this temple precisely for my present day."
idiomatic: The late emperor foresaw this; he built that temple for this day."

literal: She wished to cut her hair.
idiomatic: She reached for the shears.

literal: Suzong and the ministers were greatly afraid; they knocked their heads and wept, earnestly and bitterly begging.
idiomatic: Suzong and the ministers were terrified; they knocked their heads and wept and begged.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling's voice and bearing were very stern; her intent would not turn.
idiomatic: Ling's voice was harsh; she would not relent.

literal: Suzong then lodged at Jiafu Hall for several days and secretly plotted with the empress dowager against Cha.
idiomatic: Suzong lodged at Jiafu for days and secretly plotted with Ling against Cha.

literal: Within, Suzong plotted against him, but outwardly he grew stricter; the empress dowager's angry words and her wish to go back and forth to Xianyang—all were told to Cha.
idiomatic: Within, Suzong plotted; outwardly he grew stricter; Ling's anger and her wish to visit Xianyang were all told to Cha.

literal: He also wept before Cha, telling of the empress dowager's wish to leave the household and his fearful heart.
idiomatic: He wept before Cha too, telling how Ling meant to take the tonsure and how afraid he was.

literal: Such secret words came several times a day.
idiomatic: Such secret talk came several times a day.

literal: Cha was not suspicious in the least and instead urged Suzong to follow the empress dowager's intent.
idiomatic: Cha suspected nothing and urged Suzong to yield to Ling.

literal: Thereupon the empress dowager often held court at Xianyang; the two palaces were no longer blocked.
idiomatic: Then Ling often held court at Xianyang; the two palaces were no longer barred.

literal: Cha promoted his kinsman Yuan Faseng to Inspector of Xuzhou; Faseng seized the province in rebellion; Empress Dowager Ling repeatedly spoke of it; Cha was deeply ashamed and repentant.
idiomatic: Cha made his kinsman Yuan Faseng Xuzhou inspector; Faseng rebelled and held the province; Ling spoke of it again and again; Cha was ashamed.
